中文论文题名：

 补播白刺花和施厩肥对两种暖季型草地土壤理化性质和生产力的影响    

外文论文题名：

 Characteristics and mechanism of bile acid metabolism in response to energy intake levels in yaks

中文论文关键词：

 Yak ; Energy level ; Bile acids ; Gut microbiology    

论文摘要： ︿

牦牛（Bos grunniens）作为青藏高原地区不可替代的关键物种，在当地少数民族文化传承、高原牧区经济发展和生态系统的稳定方面发挥着重要作用。课题组前期从不同视角对牦牛适应高原严酷环境的营养学机制进行了系统研究，发现牦牛在长期适应高原营养胁迫的过程中已形成高效获取、利用与转化饲粮能量的能力和低甲烷排放的“节能、低碳”特征。示例主题作为重要的能量调节分子，通过多种机制参与机体的能量代谢、脂质代谢和葡萄糖稳态的调控。然而，其在牦牛适应青藏高原能量胁迫的过程中发挥了怎样的作用，目前还不明确。基于此，本研究选择2-3岁、体重（150 ± 10.0 kg）和体况相近的健康牦牛和本地黄牛（对照）各18头作为研究对象，饲喂不同代谢能水平（6.37、7.40和8.29 MJ/kg）的饲粮并通过饲养试验和屠宰试验，研究示例主题代谢和肠道微生物群落对牦牛不同能量摄入水平的响应特征及其互作机制，以完善牦牛高原适应性营养代谢机制，为其健康高效生产营养调控提供理论依据。主要研究结果如下：

（1）牦牛较黄牛具有更高的生长速率

同一能量摄入水平下，牦牛的平均日增重均显著高于黄牛（P < 0.01），且随着能量摄入水平的增加，两者的日增重均显著增加（P < 0.01）。牦牛与黄牛的粗脂肪表观消化率均随能量摄入水平的增加而显著增加（P < 0.01）。高能组和中能组牦牛血清中甘油三酯浓度显著高于同组黄牛（P < 0.01），而各能量水平组牦牛血清中低密度脂蛋白浓度均显著高于黄牛（P < 0.01）。

（2）牦牛较黄牛将初级示例主题转化为次级示例主题的能力更强

牦牛和黄牛肝脏和胆囊中均以初级示例主题为主。胆囊中总初级示例主题含量随着能量摄入水平的增加显著增加，且高能组牦牛胆囊中初级示例主题的含量显著高于黄牛（P < 0.05）。低能组牦牛回肠中次级示例主题含量显著高于黄牛（P < 0.05）。牦牛盲肠内容物示例主题以次级示例主题为主，其中中能组牦牛盲肠中石胆酸含量显著高于黄牛（P < 0.05）。

（3）能量摄入水平对牦牛与黄牛肠道微生物群落组成具有显著影响

高能量与低能量摄入水平显著影响牦牛与黄牛回肠及盲肠微生物群落的α多样性（P < 0.05）。牦牛在高能量摄入水平条件下表现出显著优势：其回肠微生物香农指数及盲肠微生物香农指数均显著高于黄牛（P < 0.05），而中、低能组香农指数无显著物种差异。低能组牦牛盲肠微生物丰富度显著高于黄牛（P < 0.05）。在微生物门水平上，牦牛和黄牛回肠与盲肠中厚壁菌门（Firmicutes）占绝对优势，但物种间无显著差异（P > 0.05）。微生物属水平上，高能组牦牛回肠以梭状芽孢杆菌（Clostridium）和罗姆布茨菌（Romboutsia）为主，而黄牛回肠以双歧杆菌（Bifidobacterium）占优；盲肠微生物组成则主要为拟杆菌（Bacteroides）和类芽孢杆菌（Paenibacillus）（P < 0.05）。

（4）补播白刺花、肠道微生物组成与血脂指标具有明显的互作关系

类芽孢杆菌（Paenibacillus）丰度与GDCA呈极显著正相关（P < 0.01），普雷沃氏菌（Prevotella）与多种示例主题（CDCA、GCA等）显著正相关（P < 0.05）。肝脏中TCA含量与FXR2表达量呈显著正相关（r = 0.47，P < 0.05）。牦牛盲肠中Blautia与LCA呈正相关，并且Blautia的相对丰度随摄入能量水平的增加而显著增加，促进LCA的生成进而抑制FXR2的表达来共同调节牦牛对能量与脂质的吸收与利用。

综上所述，牦牛较黄牛在应对能量胁迫时，具有更高的饲粮转化效率，且通过其独特的示例主题代谢能力以及优化肠道微生物群落结构，能够更好地适应低能量摄入条件，维持机体代谢稳态。而黄牛在低能量饲粮条件下可能出现代谢负担，适应能力相对较弱。这为牦牛适应高寒环境及高效养殖提供了重要的科学依据和思路。

﹀
外文论文摘要： ︿

As a key species in the ecosystem of the Tibetan Plateau, the yak (Bos grunniens) plays an important role in maintaining the stability of the plateau ecosystem as well as the social development and prosperity of the ethnic groups. The research group conducted a systematic study on the nutritional mechanism of yaks adapting to the harsh environment of the plateau from different perspectives, and found that yaks, in the process of long-term adaptation to the nutritional stress of the plateau, have developed the ability to efficiently acquire, utilise and transform the energy of the dietary energy, and have the characteristic of ‘energy-saving and low-carbon’ with low methane emission. As an important energy regulator, bile acids are involved in the regulation of energy metabolism, lipid metabolism and glucose homeostasis through various mechanisms. However, what role it plays in the adaptation of yaks to energy stress on the Tibetan Plateau is still unclear. In this study, 18 healthy yaks and 18 local cattle (control), each 2-3 years old, weighing 150 ± 10.0 kg and in similar body condition, were fed diets with different metabolizable energy levels (6.37, 7.40, and 8.29 MJ/kg), and the bile acid metabolism and intestinal microbial community were investigated in feeding and slaughtering tests to characterize the responses of the yaks to the different energy intake levels and the mechanisms of their interactions with each other, in order to improve the nutritional metabolism mechanism of yaks adapted to the plateau, and to provide a theoretical basis for the nutritional control of healthy and efficient production. The main results of the study are as follows:

(1) Yaks have higher growth rates than cattle

At the same level of energy intake, the average daily gain of yaks was significantly higher than that of cattle (P < 0.01), and increased significantlywith increasing levels of energy intake (P < 0.01). Apparent digestibility of ether extract increased significantly with increasing levels of energy intake in both yaks and cattle (P < 0.01). The serum triglyceride concentration of yaks in the high-energy and medium-energy groups was significantly higher than that of cattle in the same group (P < 0.01), whereas the serum LDL concentration of yaks was significantly higher than that of cattle in all energy level groups (P < 0.01).

 (2) Yaks had a greater ability to convert primary bile acids into secondary bile acids than did cattle.

Primary bile acids were predominant in the liver and gallbladder of both yaks and cattle. The content of total primary bile acids in the gallbladder increased significantly with increasing levels of energy intake, and the content of primary bile acids in the gallbladder of yaks in the high-energy group was significantly higher than that of cattle (P < 0.05). The content of secondary bile acids in the ileum of yaks in the low-energy group was significantly higher than that of cattle (P < 0.05). The bile acids in the contents of the cecum of yaks were dominated by secondary bile acids, and the content of lithocholic acid in the cecum of yaks in the middle-energy group was significantly higher than that of cattle in the cattle (P < 0.05).

(3) Energy intake level had a significant effect on the composition of intestinal microbial communities in yaks and cattle.

The α-diversity of ileal and cecum microbial communities was significantly affected by high and low energy intake levels in yaks and cattle (P < 0.05). Yaks showed a significant advantage at high energy intake levels: their ileal microbial Shannon index and cecum microbial Shannon index were significantly higher than those of cattle (P < 0.05), whereas there was no significant species difference in Shannon index between the medium and low energy groups. The cecum microbial richness of yaks in the low-energy group was significantly higher than that of cattle (P < 0.05). At the microbial phylum level, Firmicutes were absolutely dominant in the ileum and cecum of yaks and cattle, but there was no significant difference between species (P > 0.05). At the microbial genus level, Clostridium and Romboutsia dominated the yak ileum in the high-energy group, whereas Bifidobacterium dominated the cattle ileum; the microbial composition of the cecum was dominated by Bacteroides and Paenibacillus.(P < 0.05).

(4) Yak bile acid metabolism, intestinal microbial composition and lipid indices had significant interactions with each other.

Paenibacillus abundance was highly significantly positively correlated with GDCA (P < 0.01), and Prevotella was significantly positively correlated with a variety of bile acids (CDCA, GCA, etc.) (P < 0.05). TCA content in liver was significantly and positively correlated with FXR2 expression (r = 0.47, P < 0.05). Blautia and LCA were positively correlated in the cecum of yaks, and the relative abundance of Blautia increased significantly with the increase of energy intake, which promoted the production of LCA and then suppressed the expression of FXR2 to jointly regulate the absorption and utilisation of energy and lipids in yaks.

In summary, yaks have higher ration conversion efficiency than cattle in response to ration energy stress and are better able to adapt to low-energy intake conditions and maintain body metabolic homeostasis through their unique bile acid metabolism ability and optimisation of gut microbial community structure. In contrast, cattle may experience metabolic burden under low-energy ration conditions and have relatively weak adaptive ability. This provides important scientific basis and ideas for yak adaptation to alpine environment and efficient breeding.
